thread.title: Charting a bullish Q4 start, S&P 500 rises to challenge record close

author: Michael Ashbaugh
title: Charting a bullish Q4 start, S&P 500 rises to challenge record close
text:
Editor’s Note: This is a free edition of The Technical Indicator, a daily MarketWatch subscriber newsletter. To get this column each market day, click here.
Though the bigger-picture backdrop is not one-size-fits-all, the big three U.S. benchmarks are off to a bullish fourth-quarter start.
Consider that each index — the S&P 500, Dow industrials and Nasdaq Composite — topped Monday almost on its all-time closing high, areas that remain within striking distance to start October.
Before detailing the U.S. markets’ wider view, the S&P 500’s SPX, +0.23% hourly chart highlights the past two weeks.
As illustrated, the S&P has maintained its breakout point, an area spanning from 2,913 to 2,916. Last week’s brief whipsaw lower was fueled by the Federal Reserve’s policy statement.
This week’s upturn places the S&P’s record close (2,930.75) and absolute record peak (2,940.91) within view.
Similarly, the Dow Jones Industrial Average has rallied toward the range top.
Its record close (26,743.50) and absolute record peak (26,769.16) remain just overhead.
Conversely, a near-term inflection point closely matches the January peak (26,616).
Against this backdrop, the formerly lagging Nasdaq Composite COMP, +0.12% has also come to life.
Consider that Monday’s session high (8,107.4) missed the Nasdaq’s record close (8,109.7) by just two points.
The index has subsequently pulled in to its breakout point (8,042), an area also illustrated below. The retest remains underway.
Widening the view to six months adds perspective.
On this wider view, the Nasdaq has maintained trendline support, rising to challenge the range top (8,042).
The index started October with a breakout attempt that remains underway. On further strength, its record close (8,109.69) is closely followed by the absolute record peak (8,133.30).
Looking elsewhere, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is acting well technically.
Recall that the September breakout was directionally sharp, encompassing three straight closes atop the 20-day volatility bands (not illustrated). See the Sept. 25 review.
The subsequent pullback has been comparably flat, positioning the Dow to extend its breakout. The blue-chip benchmark gapped higher to start October, rising within striking distance of record territory.
Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has survived a jagged retest of its breakout point.
The specific area spans from about 2,913 to 2,916, and is followed by the ascending 20-day moving average, currently 2,904.
The bigger picture As detailed above, the big three U.S. benchmarks are starting the fourth quarter on a bullish note. Consider the following:
The Dow industrials topped Monday six points under its all-time closing high (26,743.5). The Nasdaq Composite topped Monday two points under its corresponding record close (8,109.7). The S&P 500 topped Monday six points above its record close (2,930.75). Put differently, each index challenged its record close on Monday, Oct. 1, the fourth quarter’s first session. Constructive price action.
Moving to the small-caps, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF’s IWM, -0.57% backdrop remains a fly in the soup.
Still, recall that the small-caps outperformed to start 2018 as the group is comparably insulated from trade-related headwinds. Its prevailing downturn has surfaced as trade tensions unwind.
Technically, the small-cap benchmark has violated its breakout point (170.20) and the 50-day moving average, currently 169.10.
Deeper support matches the mid-August low (165.15). A violation would mark a “lower low” raising a technical caution flag.
Similarly, the SPDR S&P MidCap 400 has ventured under notable support.
The specific area matches its breakout point (366.70), a level closely matching trendline support.
Here again, the MDY’s downturn raises the flag to an intermediate-term trend shift. Tactically, the pending retest of the trendline, from underneath, should be a useful bull-bear gauge.
Meanwhile, the SPDR Trust S&P 500 continues to outperform the small- and mid-cap benchmarks.
The prevailing upturn places its record close (293.58) and absolute record peak (293.94) firmly within striking distance.
Placing a finer point on the S&P 500, its six-month backdrop remains bullish.
Recall that notable support matches its breakout point, an area spanning from 2,913 to 2,916.
The S&P concluded the third quarter, last week, with consecutive closes at 2,914. The successful retest of support is constructive.
More immediately, the very early October upturn places uncharted territory within view. Inflection points match the S&P’s record close (2,930.75) and absolute record peak (2,940.91).
As always, it’s the response to resistance that’s worth tracking. The chances of a breakout improve to the extent the S&P holds tightly to the range top, and a near-term target projects to the 2,980 area on follow-through.
See also: Bull trend pauses: S&P 500 holds the breakout point (2,916) ahead of the Fed.
Tuesday’s Watch List The charts below detail names that are technically well positioned. These are radar screen names — sectors or stocks poised to move in the near term. For the original comments on the stocks below, see The Technical Indicator Library.
Initially profiled May 7, Dow 30 component Apple, Inc. AAPL, +1.20% has returned 22.7% and remains well positioned.
The shares started August with a massive strong-volume breakout, becoming the first company to reach a $1 trillion market value after the company’s third-quarter results.
More immediately, the shares have established a flag-like pattern — an orderly five-week range, pinned to the steep August rally — positioning the shares to extend the uptrend.
Tactically, the prevailing range top (229.67) matches Apple’s all-time high, and is currently under siege. A near-term target projects to the 241 area on follow-through.
Conversely, initial support matches the range bottom, circa 216.60, and is closely followed by the 50-day moving average, a level that has defined the prevailing uptrend. Apple’s intermediate-term bias remains bullish barring a violation.
Looking elsewhere, the United States Oil Fund USO, -0.38% — profiled last week, and revisited Monday — has extended its breakout. The fund tracks the price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) light, sweet crude oil.
Specifically, the shares have reached nearly three-year highs, placing distance atop trendline resistance and the July peak.
The breakout opens the path to less-charted territory, illustrated on the four-year chart , and potentially material longer-term follow-through. An intermediate-term target continues to project to the 17.10 area.
Conversely, the breakout point (15.25) pivots to support, and the USO’s intermediate-term technical bias remains firmly bullish barring a violation.
Moving to U.S. sectors, the VanEck Vectors Oil Services ETF OIH, +0.35% has turned higher amid crude oil’s resurgence.
As illustrated, the group has cleared trendline resistance, rising to challenge the 200-day moving average.
Underlying the upturn, its relative strength index (not illustrated) has recently notched four-month highs, improving the chances of eventual follow-through. Tactically, support matches the former breakdown point (24.70) and the group’s recovery attempt is intact barring a violation.
Caterpillar, Inc. CAT, +1.92% is another Dow 30 component (along with Apple) coming to life. (Yield = 2.3%.)
The chart above is a one-year view. Each bar still represents one session.
As illustrated, the shares have rallied atop trendline resistance, and the 200-day moving average, signaling a primary trend shift.
Underlying the upturn, its relative strength index (not illustrated) has recently tagged its best levels since January, improving the chances of incremental follow-through. Tactically, the 200-day moving average (149.40) is closely followed by the former range top (146.70) and the rally attempt is intact barring a violation.
Finally, Owens-Illinois, Inc. OI, +1.60% is a mid-cap manufacturer of bottles and glass containers. (Demand for packaging products tends to pick up amid a strengthening economy.)
The shares initially spiked two months ago, staging a mid-July spike after the company’s second-quarter results. More recently, the shares have knifed to five-month highs, rising after an activist investor encouraged the company to sell its European division.
By comparison, the prevailing pullback has been orderly, placing the shares at attractive entry near the breakout point (18.70) and 7.6% under the September peak.
